title: The Flower Lover
text:
In the Valkeri mountains

among the strutting peacocks

I found a flower

as big as my head

and when I stretched out

to smell it

I lost my earlobe

part of my nose

one eye

and half the pack

of cigarettes


I went back

the next day

intending to cut

that damned thing

down

but I found it

so beautiful

that instead

I killed a

peacock.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the deadpan violence and the absurd substitution of killing the peacock instead of the flower.

title: The Tigress
text:
Terrible arguments.

and, finally, lying peacefully

in her long bed

printed

in red with fresh flower designs,

my head and belly down

head to the sides

bathed by dull light

while she bathes silently in the

other room,

everything goes beyond me,

like most things,

I hear classical music on the little radio,

she bathes, I hear the sound of water.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the quiet aftermath of argument and the speaker's passive listening from the bed.

title: Love, Fame and Death
text:
It sits outside my window

like an old woman going to market;

it sits and watches me,

sweats nervously

through wire and fog and dog-bark

until unexpectedly

I strike the screen with a newspaper

as if swatting a fly

and you could hear the scream

in this ordinary city,

and then it left.


the way to end a poem

like this

is to suddenly grow

silent.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the strange watcher outside the window and the self-conscious abrupt ending.

title: Fast Food
text:
I

Took

My

Friend

To

Your

Latest

Poetry

Reading,

She

Told

Me,

And

What?

And

What?,

I

Asked

Her.

She

Is

Young

And

Beautiful,

She

Told

Me.

And

So?,

I

Asked

Her.

She

Can't

Stand

Your

Boldness.

Then

She

Stretched

Out

On

The

Sofa

And

Took

Off

Her

Boots.

I

Don't

Have

Very

Pretty

Legs,

She

Said.

Well,

I

Thought,

I

Don't

Make

Very

Pretty

Poetry

And

She

Doesn't

Have

Very

Pretty

Legs.

Two

Scrambled!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the one-word-per-line pacing and the final scrambled-eggs punchline.

title: Oh, Forgive Me For Whom the Bell Tolls
text:
oh, forgive me For Whom the Bell Tolls,

oh, forgive me Man Who Walked on Water,

oh, forgive me old woman who lived in a shoe,

oh, forgive me the mountain that roared at midnight,

oh, forgive me the mute sounds of night and day and death,

oh, forgive me the death of the last beautiful panther,

oh, forgive me all sunken ships and defeated armies,

this is my first FAX POEM.

It is too late:

I have

fallen

in love.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the catalogue of mock invocations and the late comic confession of love.
